$comment: Everyday stories, noun Concept, part 1 of 4 (actionMetadata, aggregateBalance, aggregateCollection, aggregateCollectionLookupField, aggregateInvariant, composition). Same style rules as stories-pilot.json. Owner reviews each part.

stories.actionMetadata.confirmationText: A bank clerk is about to close a customer's account and one slip of the finger could cancel the wrong one. The confirmation text is the question the app asks first, such as 'Close the account of Ana Souza for good?'. The action only runs after the person answers yes.
stories.actionMetadata.dangerLevel: A kitchen has a 'refill the salt' button and a 'throw away the whole fridge' button, and they should not feel alike. Danger level tells the app how serious a button is, from low to critical. The more serious it is, the louder the warning colours and the confirmation around it.
stories.actionMetadata.label: On a lift's panel the buttons say 'Open door', not 'Execute procedure 7'. The label is the word written on the action's button, in plain language and in each language the app supports. People press what they understand.
stories.actionMetadata.permissionHint: A trainee presses 'Approve' and is told no, without any reason. The permission hint is the sentence that explains which permission the action needs, such as 'Only managers can approve refunds'. The person knows who to ask instead of guessing.
stories.actionMetadata.visibleWhen: A 'Cancel booking' button makes no sense on a trip that has already ended. This rule is a short condition, and the button is shown only while it is true. When the situation changes, the button simply is not there, so nobody can press it by mistake.
stories.aggregateBalance.collection: A warehouse transfer has a list of rows, some leaving one shelf and some arriving at another. This keyword tells the balance rule which list of rows to check, including a list that sits inside another list, such as the positions inside each line of the order.
stories.aggregateBalance.discriminatorField: On a transfer slip, each row says 'From' or 'To'. The discriminator is the box that says which side a row is on. The balance rule reads it to know which quantities go into the left pile and which into the right pile.
stories.aggregateBalance.groupBy: Moving 10 apples and 5 pears is balanced only if 10 apples left and 10 apples arrived. Group by tells the rule to count separately for each product, or each product and expiry date. Without it, the whole list would be one single pile.
stories.aggregateBalance.leftValue: The slip uses the word 'Origin' for rows where goods leave. Left value is that exact word. The balance rule adds up every row marked with it and compares the total with the other side.
stories.aggregateBalance.message: When the transfer does not add up, the clerk should read 'Missing 3 units of Apples', not a code. The message is that sentence, with the missing amount and the product filled in. If you leave it out, the app writes a plain one for you.
stories.aggregateBalance.name: Each rule needs a name, because when it stops a save the error says which rule did it, for example 'stock-transfer-balance'. The name is required and cannot be repeated inside the same document, so the person fixing it knows exactly which check complained.
stories.aggregateBalance.quantityField: To check that what left equals what arrived, the app must know which box holds the amounts. The quantity field names it. The balance rule adds up that box on each side, group by group, and compares the totals.
stories.aggregateBalance.rightValue: The slip uses 'Destination' for rows where goods arrive. Right value is that exact word, and it must differ from the left one. The balance rule adds up the rows marked with it and checks that they match what left.
stories.aggregateCollection.childField: An order line must always say which order it belongs to. The child field is that 'belongs to' box on each line. It is how the app finds all lines of one order when it opens it and writes them back with it.
stories.aggregateCollection.collections: An order has lines, and each line may have several storage positions inside it, like a box with smaller boxes in it. This keyword lists the smaller lists nested inside a list, so they are opened and saved together with it.
stories.aggregateCollection.concept: A document is more than its header: an invoice has lines. This keyword says which kind of record the lines are, such as 'InvoiceLine'. Every record of that kind that belongs to the document becomes part of the list.
stories.aggregateCollection.lookupFields: While you fill an order line, you also want to see how many are left in stock, but stock is not part of the line. A lookup field is a read-only note fetched from somewhere else when the list opens. It is shown but never saved with the line.
stories.aggregateCollection.name: A document with several lists needs a name for each one, like 'lines' or 'payments'. The name is the list's address inside the document, and a list inside a list is reached with a dot, such as 'lines.positions'.
stories.aggregateCollection.orderBy: The lines of a delivery note should appear in the order of the shelves, not in the order of the day someone typed them. Order by names the box that sorts the rows of the list. Everyone then sees them in the same sequence.
stories.aggregateCollection.ownership: Order lines belong to the order: if the order is thrown away, so are they. Customers listed on a mailing do not: they exist on their own and are only linked. Ownership says which one it is. Owned rows are created and deleted with the document; referenced ones are only linked.
stories.aggregateCollectionLookupField.joinField: To show the stock next to each order line, the app must match a line to its stock row. The join field is the box that exists on both and holds the same value, such as the product code. Rows with equal values are paired when the list opens.
stories.aggregateCollectionLookupField.name: The extra information shown beside each line needs a label of its own, such as 'available'. The name is the box under which the looked-up value appears on every loaded row. It is shown, but never stored with the line.
stories.aggregateCollectionLookupField.query: The 'available stock' figure has to come from somewhere. This keyword names the saved question, such as 'stock per product', that the app asks once when the list opens, then pairs its answers with the rows.
stories.aggregateCollectionLookupField.valueFiel: The saved question answers with several columns, but you only want one, say 'quantityOnHand'. The value field picks that column from the matching answer and shows it under the lookup's name.
stories.aggregateInvariant.expression: A delivery must never carry more boxes than the truck holds. The expression is that rule written as a one-line condition over the whole document, such as every line has a quantity above zero and the total fits the capacity. If it is false, nothing is saved.
stories.aggregateInvariant.message: When a document breaks a rule, the person should read 'The truck cannot carry more than 40 boxes', not a technical complaint. The message is that sentence. If you leave it out, the app builds a plain one from the rule's name.
stories.aggregateInvariant.name: When a rule stops a save, the error must say which rule it was, such as 'truck-capacity'. The name is required and unique inside the document. It is what the person, and anyone reading logs, will see when something is refused.
stories.composition.balances: In a warehouse transfer, what leaves must equal what arrives, product by product. Balance rules state that, and the app checks it when saving, or on demand from a button without saving anything. A transfer that does not add up is refused with a clear message.
stories.composition.collections: A purchase order is one thing to the buyer, but in the database it is a header and many lines. Collections list the lines that travel with the header: they are opened together, edited together and saved together, so no one ever sees half an order.
stories.composition.invariants: Some rules involve the whole document, not one box: the sum of the line amounts must equal the invoice total. Invariants are those rules. They run just before saving, and if one fails the error names it and nothing at all is written.
stories.composition.metadata: Sometimes the author wants to leave a note on the document's structure for colleagues or tools, such as 'owned by the billing team'. Metadata is a free notebook. The app carries it along untouched and does not act on it.
stories.composition.onCommit: Once an order and all its lines are saved, someone has to reserve the stock. This keyword names the flow that runs right after the saving, in the same breath. If it fails, everything is undone, so the order is never saved half-done.
stories.composition.onValidate: Before an order is written, a clerk would check that the customer is not blocked. This keyword names a flow that runs first, inside the same saving. If it says no, nothing at all is written, not even the header.
